opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think FP8 is one of those things that sounds like a low-level engineering detail, but it actually matters a lot for scale. At the end of the day, what you care about is how much useful compute you can get out of a fixed budget of GPUs and time. If you can do your matrix multiplications in FP8 instead of BF16, you roughly double your theoretical throughput on hardware that supports it, and you reduce memory and communication pressure. That translates directly into either training a bigger model or training the same model on more tokens, and we've seen again and again that both of those help.

That said, it's not free. When we were working on Llama, the hard part was never "can we make it run in FP8," it was "can we make it run in FP8 and still trust the loss curve at scale." Lower precision introduces instabilities, especially when you go to very large runs. You get outliers in activations, some layers are much more sensitive than others, and things that look fine at a small scale can diverge after weeks of training. So in practice you end up with mixed approaches: keep certain components in higher precision, use careful scaling factors, sometimes per-tensor or finer-grained scaling, and monitor very closely. And when you're running on tens of thousands of GPUs, a divergence is extremely expensive, so the risk calculus is real.

I also think it's useful to separate training and inference. For inference, quantization is already very mature: FP8, INT8, even 4-bit, and the community has done amazing work there. That's huge for making these models usable by everyone, including running them locally. For training, it's moving more slowly because the bar for stability is so much higher, but the direction is clear. Hardware is going that way, the recipes are getting better, and I expect lower precision training to become the default rather than the exception.

And more broadly, I see it as part of a bigger story: scaling isn't just about adding GPUs. It's about squeezing more efficiency out of every layer of the stack: precision, parallelism, data quality, architecture. FP8 is one of those multipliers, and when you stack multipliers, that's how you get the next order of magnitude.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. When you train at the scale we were training Llama 3, the bottleneck is really the number of FLOPs you can push through the cluster in a given time. And FP8 is basically a way to get more effective compute out of the same hardware. On H100s you can roughly double your throughput compared to BF16, which at the scale of tens of thousands of GPUs is a massive deal. It's not a small efficiency gain, it's the difference between training a model in a few months or waiting much longer.

But it's not free. The tricky part with FP8 is numerical stability. When you go to lower precision, you lose dynamic range, and so you need to be careful about which parts of the computation you quantize. Typically you keep the master weights, the optimizer states, the gradient accumulation in higher precision, and you quantize the matrix multiplications, which is where most of the compute is anyway. And you need good scaling strategies so that you don't get overflow or underflow in the activations. This is why in the Llama 3 paper we were quite conservative, we used FP8 more for inference, and we were careful with the training recipe because at that scale, if you get a loss spike or a divergence after weeks of training, it's extremely costly.

So the way I see it, there's a kind of trajectory. The industry went from FP32 to mixed precision with FP16, then BF16 became the standard, and now FP8 is becoming the next step. And there's already research on FP4 and even more aggressive formats. Each step gives you more scale for the same cost, but each step also requires more engineering to keep training stable. The models we train are very sensitive to these details.

What I find interesting too is that this interacts with the scaling laws. If you can get twice the compute, the question is how you spend it. More tokens, bigger models, more training time. And with Llama 3 we were already training way past the Chinchilla optimal point, because what matters in the end is inference cost, not just training cost. So quantization helps on both sides. It helps you train bigger and longer, and then it helps you serve the model cheaply. For me that's the real contribution. It's not just a technical trick, it changes the economics of the whole pipeline, and it's one of the reasons why open models can keep up with the frontier.

astra-6.text:
I think FP8 is one of those improvements that looks like an implementation detail but actually matters a lot for scaling. If you can train at lower precision, you reduce memory usage and move less data, and on hardware that supports it well, you get more compute throughput. So for the same budget, you can run more experiments or train a larger model or train on more tokens.

The challenge is preserving stability. Training is different from inference: you’re making updates over billions or trillions of tokens, and numerical errors can affect that trajectory. So it’s usually mixed precision—you use FP8 where it works, with appropriate scaling, and keep higher precision where you need it.

What’s exciting is that these gains compound with improvements in architectures, kernels, and distributed training. Lower precision doesn’t solve scaling by itself, but it lets you get substantially more useful work out of the hardware you already have.

sol-6.1.text:
I think FP8 is a very important direction because it lets you reduce the memory and compute required for training. At the scale we’re talking about, those savings matter enormously: with the same hardware budget, you can train a larger model or process more tokens.

The challenge is making sure you preserve training stability and model quality. You can’t necessarily use the same precision everywhere; some operations are more sensitive than others. So the question is where you can go to lower precision and where you need to keep higher precision.

If you can get essentially the same quality at a lower cost, that’s a very powerful way to scale. It’s complementary to getting more GPUs or improving the architecture—you’re making the hardware you already have more efficient.
